question: What does CLIP learn from image-caption pairs?
options: To generate captions word by word
An image encoder and a text encoder whose embeddings are close for matching pairs
To segment objects in images
To translate captions into other languages
explanation: CLIP trains two encoders into a shared space with a contrastive objective; it does not generate text.

question: Why are CLIP embeddings L2-normalized before the dot product?
options: So the dot product is cosine similarity and only direction matters
To make the model smaller
Because images have no magnitude
To remove the temperature
explanation: Normalized vectors give dot products in [-1, 1], comparable across modalities; the temperature then sets the scale.

question: In a batch of N pairs, what are the targets for the row-wise cross-entropy of the similarity matrix?
options: All zeros
The class labels of the images
The indices 0..N-1, so each image's target is its own caption on the diagonal
Random indices
explanation: Image i was paired with caption i, so each row is classified against arange(N); the column-wise loss does the same for captions.

question: Training loss plateaued near 2.6 with batch 128 and 10 digit classes. Why?
options: The learning rate was too high
The temperature was frozen
The image encoder was too small
About 14 captions per batch describe each image equally well, so the best achievable loss is about ln 14
explanation: Same-class captions are false negatives; the model can only spread probability over them, which gives a floor near ln(14).

question: How does CLIP perform zero-shot classification?
options: It fine-tunes on a few labeled examples
It embeds a text prompt per class and picks the class with the highest cosine similarity to the image
It clusters the images with k-means
It generates a caption and parses the label
explanation: Class names become prompts like 'a handwritten seven'; their embeddings act as the weights of a classifier built from text.

question: What does a linear probe measure?
options: How linearly separable the classes are in the frozen embedding space
The speed of the text encoder
The temperature of the softmax
The number of false negatives
explanation: Training only a linear classifier on frozen features shows how much class information the representation already exposes.
